newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bkk Bank of Commerce may face delisting.
newsitem.headline: Bkk Bank of Commerce may face delisting.

text.p: The Stock Exchange of Thailand said on Friday that the troubled and suspended Bangkok Bank of Commerce Plc's deteriorating financial position makes it a candidate for delisting.

The Thai bourse said in a statement that the bank, taken over by the government last May, had reported outstanding net worth and tangible assets amounting to less than 50 percent of its 35.5 billion baht (paid up capital.
The bank, suspended from trading since May 1996, on Friday reported a huge 24.8 billion baht net loss for last year against a 860.4 million baht profit for 1995.

The exchange said in compliance with its regulations, it would give bank shareholders and investors a chance to trade Bangkok Bank of Commerce shares between April 17 and May 16 before it decides whether to delist the bank. From May 19, the share would be suspended again.
The bank said earlier it had outstanding loans and interest receivables amounting to 87.1 billion baht at end-1996 against 64.4 billion baht a year ago.
The government took over the ailing bank in May 1996 to save it from a massive run on its deposits after it was found saddled with big debts.

Thai police recently issued warrants of arrest for the bank's former president Krirkkiat Jalichandra, former adviser Rakesh Saxena and Saudi Arabian tycoon Adnan Khashoggi on charges of trying to defraud the bank.

The central bank has asked the Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand to manage the ailing bank for seven years. The industrial financing bank has been given an option to initially buy an 18 percent equity stake in the bank.
Bangkok Bank of Commerce told the bourse on Friday its net non-performing loans, after collateral deduction, rose to 53.78 billion baht at end-1996 from 36.58 billion a year ago.
It said the bank, partly on an instruction by the central bank, set aside 27.2 billion baht of provisions to cover sour loans last year against 3.2 billion in 1995.
